description:
## Why this ticket exists

RELEASE GATES, run day-1 of v0.2 **before committing the service architecture**. `product-architecture-2026-07-30.md` (sections "Service & data layer" and "Top risks" #6) schedules every prototype-gated design point at the start of its phase so a failed spike re-plans the design early, not late. Two independent unverified claims are gated here (both listed under "Carried unverified flags"):

- **(a) Locking primitive on macOS/Node** — round-2 Codex review established Node has no stdlib `flock`, and `O_EXCL` takeover races on unlink. The entire single-writer protocol (T-010's publish path, T-011's service single-instance guard, T-013's reader computation leases) sits on this primitive. T-010 is explicitly blocked on this ticket.
- **(b) Unix-socket peer-credential check without a native build** — round-3 review established Node has no stdlib peer-UID API, and a native dep may violate the project's zero-lifecycle-script rule (npm 12.0.2 / pnpm 10 block dependency scripts by default; v0.1's `tests-ts/contract/packaging.contract.mjs` already enforces script-free installability).

## Go/no-go questions (state the answer in writing)

1. **Locking**: *Is there a no-build locking primitive on macOS/Node 22 that survives crash, PID reuse, and unlink/recreate takeover races — and which candidate is it?* Candidate A: an audited pure-JS lockfile package (no lifecycle build). Candidate B: our own lockfile with pid + process-start-time + random owner token, plus **inode revalidation before every publish and unlock** (verify the lock pathname still refers to the owned inode). If NEITHER survives adversarial testing → the single-writer architecture is re-planned before T-010/T-011 commit.

**RESOLVED 2026-08-01: neither survived, and the re-plan produced candidate C.** Both A and B are lockfile designs, and a lock file must be RECLAIMED when its owner dies — a judgement Node's syscalls cannot make safely (no atomic compare-and-delete, no inode-conditional replace, no flock). Candidate B's failure is reproduced, not argued: `spikes/locking/lock.race.test.mjs` shows two contenders both entering, both minting the same generation, and `release()` deleting a live successor's lock. Inode revalidation does not rescue it — it is a read-then-act check with the same TOCTOU.

**Candidate C, adopted**: a write-once port allocation published via `link()` (never clobbers, and an allocation is never reclaimed — which is exactly why `link()` is right here and fatal for a lock), plus a continuously held loopback listener adopted by the publication winner. Evidence required and delivered: publication convergence under a real N-child storm with distinct provisional ports; crash release at every publication boundary via SIGKILL; foreign-port diagnosis by domain-separated challenge–response that refuses startup rather than re-allocating; and separate purpose/allocation namespaces so T-013's reader leases cannot impersonate T-011's writer singleton. This satisfies criterion 1 as amended; the original A-or-B phrasing could not be satisfied by any correct result.
2. **Socket credentials**: *Can Node read the peer UID of a Unix-domain-socket connection on macOS without a native build step?* Yes → use it. No → adopt the specified fallback: 0700 runtime dir + high-entropy 0600 auth token + constant-time comparison. Either answer is a "go" for v0.2 — the gate decides *which* credential design T-011 implements, not whether v0.2 proceeds.

## Scope

**In:**
- Adversarial prototype of the locking candidates: N-process contender storm (exactly one winner), takeover race lost by the non-owner, and impostor rejection. The adopted primitive must support two lease namespaces (writer lease; ephemeral reader computation lease) since T-013 reuses it.
  *Was:* "Adversarial prototype of both locking candidates: crash-with-stale-lock recovery, unlink/recreate takeover race, N-process contender storm (exactly one winner), lock-file-replacement caught by inode revalidation before publish/unlock, PID-reuse impostor rejected via process-start-time + owner token ... Whichever candidate survives ...".
  *Why amended (review round 13):* the acceptance criteria below were amended when candidates A and B were disproven, but this bullet — the one an implementer reads FIRST — was not, so the ticket simultaneously required and rejected the same design. Stale-lock recovery, inode revalidation before publish/unlock, and pid+start-time owner tokens are all properties of the lockfile design this gate eliminated on evidence; each names the reclaim step Node's syscalls cannot perform safely. Requiring them here would send an implementer to rebuild candidate B. The surviving properties are kept above and are covered by `spikes/locking/portlock.test.mjs` (contender storm, impostor rejection via HMAC challenge) — the adopted primitive holds a kernel-owned port, so it has no lock file to revalidate and no stale state to recover: death releases it. See the RESOLVED note under Go/no-go question 1.
- Peer-UID probe from Node 22 on macOS, plus the fallback token design if the probe fails.
- **Socket path rules** validated empirically: macOS `sun_path` ≈104-byte limit measured (test with long usernames / long home paths); symlinked parent dirs rejected; path traversal refused before any path is constructed. Delivered and covered by `spikes/socket-cred/auth.test.mjs`.
  *Was:* the same clause continuing "; stale socket probed (connect attempt) before unlinking — a crash can leave a pathname no server owns, and a live server's socket must never be unlinked."
  *Why amended (review round 14):* Scope asserted the stale-socket rule was empirically validated while acceptance criterion 5 states plainly that no probe-then-unlink logic was prototyped and carries the requirement forward to T-011. The ticket claimed delivery and non-delivery of the same safety property, and Scope is the half a downstream implementer is likely to read — so T-011 could have been built on an "already validated" guarantee that does not exist. It is now stated in one place only, as outstanding work owned by T-011. Note also that probe-then-unlink is a read-then-act TOCTOU on its own. An earlier version of this note called "unlink only while holding the singleton lock" the safe form; that is too strong and is corrected here (review round 15). The singleton lock serializes COOPERATING spendbar instances only — it does not stop an unrelated or hostile process running as the same uid from binding the pathname between the probe and the unlink, so holding it narrows the window without closing it. T-011 therefore owns a real decision, not just a relocation: either design an endpoint protocol that never deletes a pathname on the strength of an earlier observation (for example a per-instance socket path published through the write-once allocation, so no pathname is ever reused), or explicitly accept and document the residual same-uid denial-of-service. Tracked as ISS-041.

**Out:** the control-plane protocol itself (request IDs, bounded messages, status/refresh/stop/progress ops, version negotiation — T-011); the snapshot store consuming the lock (T-010); service install/launchd (T-011).

## Approach notes

- Follow the v0.1 spike precedent: `spikes/rounding/` + an npm `spike:*` script. Put candidates in e.g. `spikes/locking/` and `spikes/socket-cred/`; `package.json` `files` is a whitelist (`dist`, `README.md`) so spikes stay out of the tarball.
- v0.1's injected-deps discipline (`src/context.ts` — `RuntimeDeps` performs no I/O; everything injectable) is the template for making race/crash scenarios testable.
- Empirical baseline is n=1: macOS 26.5.1 / Apple Silicon / Node v22.18.0 (plan header). Record the environment with each measurement.

## Constraints (hard rules)

- No native compilation, no lifecycle scripts — any candidate must install and run with scripts disabled (same discipline the packaging contract test enforces).
- `usage.py` is frozen and never modified; `package.json` never carries an author field; no real transcript data or personal paths in fixtures or prototype outputs.
- Record the decision durably (repo doc or storybloq note) so T-010/T-011 consume it without re-derivation.

## Acceptance criteria

**Criteria 1, 2, 3 and 5 were AMENDED on 2026-08-01, after the gate ran and disproved the design
they presupposed.** They are rewritten below with the original text and the reason for each change
recorded inline. This is deliberate and is the point of running a gate on day 1: criteria written
before the measurement encoded the answer it was supposed to test, and four of them could not be
satisfied by any *correct* result. Amending them silently would have been the real failure; so
would reporting the ticket complete against criteria the evidence contradicts.

1. A written go/no-go decision for the locking primitive exists in the repo, naming the adopted
   primitive, with linked evidence for each adversarial scenario. Delivered:
   `docs/v0.2-prototype-findings.md`.
   *Was:* "naming the surviving candidate (A: audited pure-JS package, or B: own lockfile)".
   *Why amended:* both A and B were disproven (see the go/no-go section above). A criterion whose
   only passing answers are the two the evidence rejects cannot report a negative result, which is
   precisely the outcome this gate exists to be able to return.

2. Automated tests runnable via `npm run test:spikes` demonstrate, for the adopted primitive:
   (a) **crash release** — SIGKILL at each real publication boundary, with a fresh uninstrumented
   process still converging on the persisted port with exactly one holder;
   (b) **an N-process contender storm yielding exactly one holder**, with all losing results
   collected while the winner provably still holds the port;
   (c) **write-once allocation convergence** from N first-run children that each hold a DIFFERENT
   provisional port before any publishes;
   (d) **continuous reservation** — an adversary binding the allocated port in the window between
   publication and adoption must get `EADDRINUSE`;
   (e) **foreign-holder refusal, COMPOSED** — `startSingleton()` joins `EADDRINUSE` →
   `identifyHolder()` → decision, and tests drive that path end to end: a holder failing the
   challenge throws `PortLockForeignHolder`, a holder that cannot be identified at all throws too
   (indeterminate never collapses into either answer), and in both cases the allocation file is
   asserted **byte-identical afterwards**.
   *Added in round 6.* The criterion previously described this composed behaviour while only the
   separate primitives were tested — so the surviving mutant was any caller that receives "foreign"
   and continues, or that "recovers" by allocating a second port. Rather than narrow the criterion
   to what was already covered, the missing orchestration was built, because it is what T-011
   inherits and what the deliverable's headline claim rests on.
   *Was:* "stale-lock recovery after simulated crash; unlink/recreate takeover race lost by the
   non-owner; ... inode revalidation detecting lock-file replacement before a publish/unlock".
   *Why amended:* every one of those clauses is a property of the lockfile design that was
   rejected. The adopted primitive has no stale state to recover and no lock file to revalidate —
   the reclaim step those clauses describe is exactly the operation Node's syscalls cannot perform
   safely, and which caused the rejection. Requiring them would require rebuilding the failed
   design. The takeover race is still covered, as *negative* evidence, by
   `spikes/locking/lock.race.test.mjs`.

3. Ownership is proved by a kernel-held listener rather than by a record on disk. Tests prove that
   an unrequested close raises a named lock-loss witness and that the lock then refuses all further
   use; and that a foreign holder of the allocated port is diagnosed by domain-separated
   challenge-response (protocol id + purpose + allocation id + the challenger's 256-bit nonce) and
   refuses startup — and that refusal is exercised through `startSingleton()`, not inferred from
   the primitives (see 2(e)). The residual-window obligations this places on T-010/T-011 are
   recorded in findings section 3.5 and are binding on those tickets: every publisher must call
   `assertHeld()` immediately before its atomic commit, `onLost` must terminate or irreversibly
   disable publishing, and their suite must carry a mutant omitting that guard which fails.
   *Was:* "The lock owner record contains pid + process-start-time + random owner token, and a test
   proves a forged owner file with a reused PID but wrong start-time/token is rejected."
   *Why amended:* the adopted primitive stores no owner record at all. That is the design, not an
   omission — there is nothing to forge, nothing to reclaim, and PID reuse is therefore not in its
   threat model. A pid/start-time/token record would reintroduce the reclaim judgement that failed.

4. A runnable probe script answers whether a peer-UID read is possible from Node 22 on macOS with
   no native build, and its result is recorded; if negative, the fallback is prototyped: 0700
   runtime dir, 0600 high-entropy token file, constant-time compare, with tests refusing a wrong
   token and a wrong-permission dir. *(Unchanged, and met: `npm run spike:socket-cred`, answer NO,
   fallback prototyped in `spikes/socket-cred/auth.mjs`.)*

5. Socket path rules are empirically validated with tests: the **canonical** path is rejected
   BEFORE `listen` when its byte length exceeds 104 (limit recorded); a long-username/long-home
   simulation passes with the chosen uid-keyed short runtime path; a symlinked component strictly
   below the trusted root is rejected; traversal components are refused outright.
   *Was:* "binding fails past the measured macOS sun_path limit ... a stale socket is detected by
   probe before unlink and a live server's socket is never unlinked."
   *Why amended:* "binding fails" was measured **FALSE**, and that is the single most consequential
   finding of this gate. macOS silently truncates to 104 bytes: `listen()` succeeds, `address()`
   reports the full untruncated path, and two distinct logical paths collide onto one socket while
   every API reports success (findings section 1). A criterion requiring an error the kernel does
   not raise cannot be met by correct code; pre-bind refusal is the same safety requirement in the
   only form that is achievable.
   **NOT DELIVERED, and carried forward rather than dropped:** the stale-socket-probe-before-unlink
   clause. No probe-then-unlink logic was prototyped. It concerns the control-plane socket endpoint
   that T-011 owns, not this gate's locking primitive, and the adopted design never unlinks a
   socket at all. It is recorded here as an explicit gap rather than quietly removed, and belongs
   to T-011.

6. npm install of the prototype's dependencies with lifecycle scripts disabled succeeds (no native
   build introduced). *(Unchanged, and met: `spikes/lifecycle.test.mjs`, mutation-tested.)*

7. usage.py is untouched and package.json still has no author field (existing contract tests remain
   green). *(Unchanged, and met.)*

## Risks

**Superseded 2026-08-01 by the gate result.** The original risk read "both locking candidates could
fail adversarial testing, re-opening the single-writer service architecture and blocking
T-010/T-011". That is no longer a risk — it is what happened, and it was resolved inside this ticket
rather than escalated: both candidates failed, and candidate C (write-once port allocation +
continuously held listener) was designed, built and evidenced here. Left recorded because a risk
that materialized and was handled is more useful to a future reader than a deleted one.

Residual risks that DO still apply:
- **All empirical results are n=1** (macOS 26.5.1 / APFS / Node 22.18.0) and may not generalize
  across macOS versions or filesystems.
- **No Linux host has ever run this suite.** The platform figures in the findings doc come from
  simulating `process.platform`, which changes which tests run and nothing about the kernel — a
  distinction that concealed a real Linux-breaking port-range defect until review round 10. Tracked
  as ISS-032, and coupled to open question 2 below.
- **The downstream tickets still specify the rejected design.** T-010/T-011/T-012/T-013 carry
  lockfile, inode-revalidation and pid/owner-token language that this gate disproved, so an
  implementer following them as written would rebuild candidate B. Tracked as ISS-033 (high).
- **Simulated crash tests may not reproduce real kill-timing races**, though the matrix now
  SIGKILLs at the real filesystem boundaries via the publication hooks rather than around them.
- The third-party-dependency supply-chain risk is retired: no locking dependency was adopted.

## Open questions (owner decisions)
1. **RESOLVED by measurement, not by preference.** The original question — what audit bar applies to
   candidate A, and if both candidates pass does the owner prefer owning the lockfile (B) over a
   third-party dep (A) — is moot: both candidates were disproven, so there is nothing to choose
   between and no third-party lockfile to audit. Recorded rather than deleted because "we picked C"
   is less useful than "A and B were eliminated on evidence, so C was not a preference".
2. **STILL OPEN, and now costed.** Must the locking and socket prototypes also pass on Linux, or is
   v0.2 macOS-only? (The plan darwin-guards the menubar helper but is silent on service
   portability.) Round 10 attached a concrete price to this: if Linux is in scope, this gate's
   empirical evidence must be re-taken on a real Linux host — CI runner or container — because
   simulation is structurally incapable of testing kernel-dependent behaviour. See ISS-032.
3. **STILL OPEN.** What exact short per-user runtime dir path should the socket use? The plan fixes
   the constraint (sun_path ≤104 bytes, 0700) but not the path. The gate has since measured that
   macOS *silently truncates* rather than erroring, so this choice is load-bearing rather than
   cosmetic — the pre-bind length check refuses what the kernel would have accepted-and-corrupted.
title: v0.2 day-1 prototypes: locking primitive + socket credential check
